title: Angles beyond 90 degrees
objectives: Define sine and cosine for any angle as the height and the across-distance of a point on the unit circle
Give the signs of sine and cosine in each quadrant
Use mirror images to find values beyond 90°

screens.title: Angles beyond 90 degrees
screens.prose: In a right-angled triangle no other angle reaches 90°. Put the triangle inside a circle of radius 1, and the angle can keep turning.
The point sits on a circle of radius 1, at 30° from the horizontal axis. Its height is $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$, the side opposite the angle in the triangle.
screens.question: Drag the point to another place on the circle where it is just as high, 0.5 above the axis.

hints.text: Watch the label on the vertical segment as you drag. It reads the height.
The height is the vertical segment from the axis up to the point.
Mirror the point in the vertical axis. It moves left, but stays 0.5 high: that is 30° short of a half turn, 150°.

feedback.correct: 150° is just as high as 30°, on the other side.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a second spot where the height label reads 0.5.

byKey.start: That is where the point began, at 30°. Look for a second spot, on the left of the circle.
byKey.below: You went below the axis. The point is 0.5 from the axis there, but underneath it, so its height is −0.5.
byKey.top: Near the top the point is higher than 0.5. Keep going round, until the height drops back to 0.5.
byKey.pt: The height is not 0.5 there yet. Drag until the vertical segment reads 0.5 again.

explain.text: You mirrored the point in the vertical axis, to 150°. The height is still 0.5, so the point is just as high. Now it sits left of the axis, and no right-angled triangle has a 150° angle.

screens.prose: Turn the point all the way round with the slider. The vertical segment is the point's height. The horizontal one is its across-distance from the centre, measured along the axis.
screens.question: Where is the across-distance negative?

options.text: Where the point is left of the vertical axis, from 90° to 270°
Where the point is below the horizontal axis, from 180° to 360°
options.why: That is where the height is negative. The across-distance follows left and right, not up and down.

options.text: Nowhere: a distance cannot be negative
options.why: You read it as a length. We measure it along the axis from the centre, so left of the centre counts as negative.

hints.text: Stop the slider at 120°, then at 240°. Read the label under the horizontal segment.

feedback.correct: Left of the vertical axis, the across-distance is negative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the across-distance label as the point passes the top and the bottom.

explain.text: At 120° the across-distance reads −0.5: the point is half a unit left of the centre. It turns negative after 90° and positive again after 270°. Up and down decides the height's sign instead.

screens.prose: For a point at angle $\theta$ on a circle of radius 1, we **define** $\cos\theta$ as its across-distance and $\sin\theta$ as its height. This circle is the **unit circle**. Up to 90° it agrees with the triangle, whose hypotenuse is 1.
screens.question: The point is at 120°. Which pair is $(\cos 120^\circ, \sin 120^\circ)$?

options.why: You used $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$ and kept its sign. The point is left of the vertical axis, so its across-distance is negative.
You swapped the two values. At 120° the point is only half a unit left, but 0.87 high.
You made both negative because the angle passed 90°. The point is still above the axis, so its height is positive.

hints.text: Is the point left or right of the vertical axis? Above or below the horizontal one?
The point at 120° is the mirror image of the point at 60°, in the vertical axis.
At 60° the point is $(0.5, 0.87)$. Mirroring it keeps the height and flips the sign of the across-distance.

feedback.correct: Half a unit left of the centre, 0.87 up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the point's across-distance and height, with their signs.

explain.text: You mirrored the 60° point, $(0.5, 0.87)$, in the vertical axis. The height stays 0.87 and the across-distance becomes −0.5. So $\cos 120^\circ = -0.5$ and $\sin 120^\circ \approx 0.87$.

screens.prose: Now the point is at 225°, past the half turn. From level 1, $\sin 45^\circ \approx 0.71$.
screens.question: What is $\sin 225^\circ$? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: Is the point above or below the horizontal axis?
225° is 45° past the half turn. The point is the 45° point, turned to the opposite side of the centre.
Turning through a half turn flips both coordinates. The 45° point is 0.71 high, so this one is 0.71 below.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find how far the point is from the horizontal axis, then its sign.

byKey.no-sign: You found the size, 0.71, but the point is below the axis. Its height is negative.
byKey.zero: The point is not on an axis. It is 45° below the left-hand axis, so its height is not 0.

explain.text: The point at 225° is the 45° point turned to the opposite side of the centre. It is 0.71 below the axis, so $\sin 225^\circ \approx -0.71$. Its across-distance is −0.71 too.

screens.prose: The point is at 300°, a sixth of a turn short of a full turn.
screens.question: Select all that apply.

options.why: You may have read the sign from the size of the angle. The point is below the horizontal axis, so its height is negative.
You expected large angles to give negative values. The point is right of the vertical axis, so its across-distance is positive.

hints.text: Look at where the point is: left or right, above or below.
The point is right of the vertical axis and below the horizontal one.
Right of centre makes cosine positive. Below the axis makes sine negative.

feedback.correct: Right of centre and below the axis: cosine positive, sine negative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide each sign from the point's position, not from the angle's size.

explain.text: The point at 300° sits in the fourth quarter of the circle, right and below. So $\cos 300^\circ = 0.5$ and $\sin 300^\circ \approx -0.87$. The four quarters are called **quadrants**, numbered anticlockwise from the first.

screens.prose: On the axes the triangle collapses to a line. The point still has an across-distance and a height.
screens.question: Drag the point to where $\cos\theta = -1$.

hints.text: Cosine is the across-distance. Where is the point as far left as it can go?
The across-distance is the horizontal segment.
A half turn, 180°, puts the point at the far left of the circle, one whole unit from the centre.

feedback.correct: At 180° the point is one unit left of the centre.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the point until it is as far left as the circle allows.

byKey.bottom: You went to the bottom, where the height is −1. That is $\sin\theta = -1$, at 270°.
byKey.start: At 0° the point is one unit to the right: $\cos 0^\circ = 1$, not −1.
byKey.top: At the top the across-distance is 0. Keep turning until the point is far left.
byKey.pt: The point is not yet at the far left. Its across-distance must read −1.

explain.text: At 180° the point is $(-1, 0)$, so $\cos 180^\circ = -1$ and $\sin 180^\circ = 0$. On an axis one value is 0 and the other is 1 or −1. These are the edge cases: no triangle, but the point still gives the values.

screens.prose: Back to 150°. Past 90°, many people expect sine to turn negative, since the angle is no longer in a triangle.
screens.question: What is the sign of $\sin 150^\circ$, and why?

options.text: Negative, because the angle is past 90°
options.why: You tied the sign to the angle passing 90°. Sine is the height, and at 150° the point is above the axis.

options.text: Negative, because the point is left of the vertical axis
options.why: Being left of the axis makes the across-distance negative. That is cosine. Sine turns negative only below the horizontal axis.

options.text: Positive, because the point is above the horizontal axis

hints.text: Which segment is the sine?
Sine is the vertical segment, from the axis to the point.
The vertical segment goes up from the axis, so the height is positive: $\sin 150^\circ = 0.5$.

feedback.correct: The point at 150° is above the axis, so $\sin 150^\circ = 0.5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide the sign from where the point is, above or below the axis.

byKey.past-90: You made sine negative because the angle passed 90°. In the second quadrant the point is above the axis, so sine is positive. Only cosine has turned negative.
byKey.left: You gave sine the sign of the left-right position. That sign belongs to cosine.

explain.text: Sine is the height, so its sign asks one question: above or below the horizontal axis. In the second quadrant the point is above, so sine is positive. It was cosine that turned negative there.

screens.prose: You read every value off the point. For any angle $\theta$, the point on the unit circle is $$(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta).$$ Sine is positive above the horizontal axis. Cosine is positive right of the vertical axis.
screens.question: In which quadrant are both $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ negative?

options.why: Cosine is negative there, but the point is above the axis. Sine is positive in the second quadrant.
Sine is negative there, but the point is right of the centre. Cosine is positive in the fourth quadrant.

hints.text: You need the point left of the centre and below the axis.
Left and below is the quarter between the half turn and three quarters of a turn.

feedback.correct: Left and below: the third quadrant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Both negative means left of centre and below the axis.

explain.text: Both values are negative when the point is left of the centre and below the axis. That is the third quadrant, from 180° to 270°. The point at 240° is there.

screens.prose: On the first screen you found that 150° is as high as 30°. Now show it for any angle $\theta$ between 0° and 90°.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: The point at $\theta$ is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$, by the definition
Its mirror image in the vertical axis is $(-\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$: the height stays and the across-distance flips
The mirror image is at angle $180^\circ - \theta$, since it stops $\theta$ short of the half turn

hints.text: Start from the definition of the point at $\theta$.
Mirror the point first, then work out the angle of the mirror image.
Definition, then the mirror image's coordinates, then its angle, then read off sine and cosine.

feedback.correct: Each line follows from the one before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the point at $\theta$, then mirror it.

byKey.d4: The conclusion reads the new point's coordinates, so it comes last.
byKey.d3: Find the mirror image's coordinates before naming its angle.

explain.text: You mirrored the point and named the angle of its image. Reading the image's coordinates gives both results. With $\theta = 30^\circ$: $\sin 150^\circ = \sin 30^\circ = 0.5$ and $\cos 150^\circ = -\cos 30^\circ \approx -0.87$.

screens.prose: A desk describes a two-share hedge by one angle $\theta$. It holds £10,000.00 × $\cos\theta$ of share A and £10,000.00 × $\sin\theta$ of share B. A negative amount is a short position.
screens.question: At $\theta = 135^\circ$, what is the position in share A, in pounds?

hints.text: Share A uses $\cos 135^\circ$. Is the point left or right of the vertical axis?
The across-distance at 135° points left.
$\cos 135^\circ = -\cos 45^\circ \approx -0.7071$, so the position is £10,000.00 × −0.7071.

feedback.correct: About −£7,071.07: the desk is short share A.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply £10,000.00 by $\cos 135^\circ$, sign included.

byKey.no-sign: You found the size, £7,071.07, but dropped the sign. The point is left of the axis, so the desk is short A.
byKey.degrees: Your calculator was in radians, so it took 135 radians. Switch it to degrees: $\cos 135^\circ \approx -0.7071$.

explain.text: At 135° the point is left of the axis and above it. So the desk is short £7,071.07 of A and long £7,071.07 of B. Turning the angle past 90° is what flipped A from long to short.

ideas: On a circle of radius 1, the point at angle $\theta$ is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$: cosine across, sine up.
The signs come from the quadrant. Sine is negative only below the horizontal axis; cosine only left of the vertical axis.
Mirror images share values up to a sign: $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$ and $\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos\theta$.

formula.name: The point on the unit circle
formula.note: On the axes: $\cos 180^\circ = -1$, $\sin 270^\circ = -1$, and the other value is 0.

summary.trap: Sine is not negative in the second quadrant. The point is above the axis there; only cosine has turned negative.

quiz.prose: The point on the unit circle is at 210°.
quiz.question: What is $\sin 210^\circ$?

options.why: You used $\sin 30^\circ$ without the sign. At 210° the point is below the axis.
That is $\cos 210^\circ$, the across-distance. Sine is the height.
That is the lowest point, at 270°. At 210° the point is only half a unit below the axis.

feedback.correct: Half a unit below the axis.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the height of the point, sign included.

explain.text: 210° is 30° past the half turn, so the point is the 30° point turned to the opposite side. Its height is −0.5. So $\sin 210^\circ = -0.5$.

quiz.question: Which quadrant is the point in?

options.why: In the first quadrant both are positive. Here sine is negative, so the point is below the axis.
In the second quadrant cosine is negative, and sine is positive. That is the reverse.
In the third quadrant cosine is negative too. Here it is positive, so the point is right of centre.

feedback.correct: Right of centre and below the axis.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Positive cosine means right; negative sine means below.

explain.text: Positive cosine puts the point right of the vertical axis. Negative sine puts it below the horizontal axis. Right and below is the fourth quadrant, from 270° to 360°.

quiz.prose: Think of the point after a half turn.
quiz.question: What is $\cos 180^\circ$?

options.why: That is $\sin 180^\circ$, the height. The across-distance is a whole unit to the left.
That is $\cos 0^\circ$. A half turn sends the point to the far left, not back to the start.
That is $\cos 120^\circ$. At 180° the point is as far left as it can go.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where is the point after a half turn?

explain.text: A half turn takes the point from $(1, 0)$ to $(-1, 0)$. Its across-distance is −1. So $\cos 180^\circ = -1$ and $\sin 180^\circ = 0$.

quiz.prose: Some angles share a sine with 40°.
quiz.question: Which angle has the same sine as 40°?

options.why: You added a half turn. That sends the point below the axis, so $\sin 220^\circ = -\sin 40^\circ$.
That mirrors the point in the horizontal axis. It is as far below as 40° is above, so the sine flips sign.
$\sin 50^\circ$ equals $\cos 40^\circ$, the across-distance. We want the same height.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mirror the 40° point in the vertical axis.

explain.text: Mirroring the 40° point in the vertical axis keeps its height. The mirror image is at $180^\circ - 40^\circ = 140^\circ$. So $\sin 140^\circ = \sin 40^\circ$.
